title: When the Room Falls
premise: Tamsin Ashgrove is hired to survey Hollowmere House, a derelict property whose rooms rearrange themselves and whose appraisal figures keep changing in her own handwriting. Waiting on the porch is Wren, the imaginary friend she invented at age seven — except Wren hasn't aged, and he remembers a childhood Tamsin has spent thirty years burying: the summer her brother disappeared, and the song the children of Hollowmere sang to keep something at bay. As the house feeds on memory and identity, Tamsin discovers she was chosen as a child to be its next keeper, and that refusing means it takes someone else. To end it she must learn the song's final verse from the house itself without singing along — because whoever sings becomes part of the walls. In the climax she lets the house wear her memories like a costume, finds her brother's voice still humming inside it, and teaches him the last verse instead; the house falls silent, releasing them both, though Tamsin walks out with gaps where her childhood used to be.
about_author: Jude Marchetti is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties across the English coast before turning to horror. Their fiction explores what houses remember about the people who tried to forget them.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A routine assignment brings her to Hollowmere House, where her laser measurements return impossible numbers and her notes appear altered overnight. She keeps the lights on and counts the doors — eleven going in, twelve coming out. The beat is professional unease curdling into personal recognition.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At dawn, a small figure waits on the porch: Wren, her imaginary friend, unchanged after thirty years, greeting her by a nickname no one living knows. He says he's been keeping her room ready. The beat is the collapse of her rational worldview.

chapters.title: Doors That Count Themselves
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, interspersed with fragments of a child's diary found in the walls. The house reshapes around her routines; hallways lengthen when she hesitates. She realizes the diary is hers, in handwriting she doesn't remember learning. The beat is mounting paranoia.

chapters.title: What I Buried in Summer
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Tamsin's POV. 1994: her brother Milo, Wren, and the neighbor children sang on the porch every dusk. Then Milo went into the house during a game and never came out, and everyone insisted there had never been a Milo. The beat is grief rediscovered.

chapters.title: The Song Without an End
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Wren teaches her the verses the children sang — four of them — but refuses to sing the fifth, saying nobody remembers it, or nobody who remembers can say. She catches herself humming along and stops mid-note as the walls lean closer. The beat is dread of complicity.

chapters.title: The Client Who Isn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Her firm has no record of the Hollowmere commission; the client's phone number rings inside the house itself. Her colleague Priya visits, sees nothing wrong, and leaves repeating a phrase in a child's sing-song. The beat is isolation deepening.

chapters.title: Rooms That Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Each room replays a memory she'd rather lose — her mother's denial, the funeral no one attended, the therapist who called Milo a 'coping fantasy.' The house wears her past like a costume, flattering and distorting it. The beat is seduction by nostalgia.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, the first departure from Tamsin. He explains what he is: not imaginary, but a previous child the house hollowed and kept, given shape so the next keeper would trust him. He begs her to take the role gently. The beat is heartbreak beneath menace.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors, Twelve Doors
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She maps the house obsessively and finds the twelfth door only appears when she isn't looking directly at it — behind it, humming. Power reveals itself: the house offers her control over its rooms if she'll only accept the key. The beat is temptation sharpening into choice.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Key
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Holding the cold iron key, she feels the house obey her — doors open, lights burn, the song hushes. It is intoxicating, and she notices she's stopped thinking about leaving. Priya calls, voice thin, asking why Tamsin sounds 'like the walls.' The beat is corruption beginning.

chapters.title: Milo's Verse
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Tamsin and a faint second voice in the walls. She follows the humming to the twelfth door and hears Milo — alive in some sense, folded into the house since 1994, singing a fragment of the fifth verse through the wood. The beat is desperate hope.

chapters.title: What the House Eats
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He shows her the truth: keepers don't guard the house, they feed it, trading memories for power until nothing remains but appetite wearing their face. He shows her the previous keeper — still standing in a hallway, smiling, entirely empty. The beat is horror at the price already paid.

chapters.title: Small Surrenders
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She can't recall her mother's face anymore, then her own birthday, then the smell of rain. The house compensates with pleasant fabrications, and part of her prefers them. She writes truths on her arms to hold the line. The beat is erosion of self.

chapters.title: Priya Comes Back
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Worried, she returns uninvited and finds Tamsin radiant, hosting a dinner party for guests who cast no shadows. When Priya grabs her arm, Tamsin's skin hums with the melody. The house begins closing doors behind Priya. The beat is an outsider witnessing the trap.

chapters.title: Run, Then
chapters.summary: Priya's POV, continuing. Priya escapes through a door that shouldn't lead outside, dragging Tamsin to the threshold — but Tamsin cannot cross; the porch light holds her like a hook. Wren watches from the window, expression unreadable. The beat is the point of no return made physical.

chapters.title: The Fifth Verse Exists
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the nursery, under wallpaper layered like sediment, she finds the original sheet music — five verses, the last torn out, its stub bearing Milo's childish initials. The house rages, lights dying room by room. The beat is defiance kindling.

chapters.title: Everything the House Took
chapters.summary: Milo's POV, dreamlike and fragmented. Inside the walls he has kept himself together for thirty years by remembering outward — holding his sister's name like a rope. He has the torn verse memorized but cannot carry it alone; a verse must be sung by someone the house hasn't eaten. The beat is reunion across a wall.

chapters.title: Singing Along
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Desperate, she tries to learn the verse fast, and catches herself harmonizing — the house swelling with pleasure as her edges blur. Wren tears the music from her hands, screaming that this is exactly how it got him. The beat is self-destruction nearly completed.

chapters.title: The Costume Trick
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She understands the house's hunger: it eats what you cling to. So she offers everything willingly — every memory, laid out like clothes — letting the house dress itself in her while she stands behind the emptying, learning the verse by feel rather than voice. The beat is terrible sacrifice as strategy.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Climax. Tamsin, nearly transparent, presses her palm to the twelfth door and passes the verse to Milo wordlessly, breath to breath through the wood. Milo sings it — complete, unseduced, unmourned — and the house, built to swallow singers, swallows its own song instead. Walls buckle; doors count down from twelve to none. The beat is cathartic rupture.

chapters.title: After the Fall
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Dawn. The house is just a house — rotting, ordinary, finally appraisable. Milo steps out onto the porch, thirty years old and nine years old at once, and Wren crumbles gratefully into dust with a smile. Tamsin surveys the ruin honestly and files a demolition order. The beat is exhausted release.

chapters.title: Gaps Where Childhood Was
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Tamsin's POV, months later. She and Milo share a small flat, rebuilding a shared history from photographs and each other's accounts, since hers are gone. Sometimes she hums a tune she doesn't recognize and stops, gently, mid-note. The final image: two mugs on a windowsill, both full. The beat is bittersweet, hard-won peace.
